why_intro: In fourteen months the federal route for putting a proposal on a company's ballot has gone from routine to uncertain. Interest in how companies handle AI has kept growing anyway.
levers_intro: If the ballot route narrows further, investor influence on AI moves to these channels. The rights map shows how open each one is at each company.

levers.name: Votes against directors
levers.text: Shareholders can still vote against the directors who oversee AI risk. Where a company uses majority voting, that vote carries weight.

levers.name: Exempt solicitations
levers.text: Investors who are not seeking proxy authority can publish their case to other shareholders by filing it with the SEC. These filings show up as form PX14A6G.

levers.name: Coalitions and private engagement
levers.text: Groups of investors meet with companies directly, without anything going to a vote. Much AI disclosure progress has come this way.

levers.name: Fund holders voting directly
levers.text: Pass-through voting programs let people who own index funds choose how their share of the fund's votes is cast.

rights_intro: For each company: where it is incorporated, what its bylaws require to bring a proposal, and how much room investors would have if the SEC rescinds Rule 14a-8.
status_key: Still open means the company's own rules leave a workable path for proposals even without Rule 14a-8. Narrowing means higher thresholds, a controlling shareholder or similar limits make that path harder. Closed means the company has adopted rules that shut out most proposal filers. These ratings are this site's reading of the cited documents, not a legal opinion.
why_now_note: Emptied 2026-11-25 at the owner's request: every item is now an event in data/causality.json (texas-sb1057, sec-noaction-pause, sec-aug14-statement, dfking-2026-season, sec-14a8-rescission-proposal, vanguard-investor-choice-2026, iss-ai-proposals-2026), so the separate Policy timeline would repeat the map.
